parts: Please read /papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/research-progress/handoffs/HDA-17-AN01.md, and evaluate the research in notes 35-37. Please discuss the state of the project currently and what are the remaining obstacles.
I’ll read the handoff and notes 35–37, check their arguments against the surrounding research, and assess the project’s current position and remaining obstacles.

The notes show a substantial improvement in the error estimates: Note 35’s trial misses its budgets badly, while Note 37 brings the source-error allowances within budget at the two tested points. The remaining distinction is crucial: those are floating calculations, and they do not yet establish a certified finite region or a global approximation. I’m checking the formulas and records behind that improvement.

The main analytic steps appear sound on inspection, including the Hermite remainder, the positivity fallback, and the separate gradient caps that bring Note 37’s last failing row within budget. The global obstacle is still unresolved: blending the finite and outer fields with a spatial cutoff generally breaks holomorphy, so the required evolution identities do not automatically survive the join.
What is the join again? Perhaps it might be some kind of phase transition

The join means combining the formulas that work in different regions—the finite-source model in the middle and the asymptotic models at large time or height—into one approximation whose density, current, potential, and covariance still satisfy the required equations.

Your phase-transition idea is relevant: the earlier notes identify a narrowing transition layer near the regulator switch at \(t=64\). I’ll check how that layer relates to the joining problem. A sharp change in the limiting profile could guide the matching, but the cutoff terms still need to be accounted for.

Yes it is probably worthwhile to consider some phase transition literature and how that is handled. I know that Landau parameters, conformal field theories and anomalous dimensions are tools used in that area of research.

I’ll look at those connections, starting with finite-size scaling, crossover theory, and Landau theory, then assess whether conformal methods or anomalous dimensions fit this problem. The existing switch-layer result gives us something concrete to compare with that literature, while keeping track of which features come from the chosen regulator.
I should say order parameter for the Landau reference, also divergence of certain observables like two point functions is another characteristic

Yes—the Landau quantity is an **order parameter**. And the correlation criterion is important: typically the correlation length or susceptibility diverges, while the connected two-point function develops long-range, often power-law behavior; it need not diverge at a fixed separation.

That gives us a useful test here: distinguish a change in the averaged profile from growing correlations in the underlying field. The project’s \(Q\) is a local filtered covariance, so we would need to establish its relation to a two-point correlation or susceptibility before interpreting it as evidence of criticality.

The closest literature connection is **finite-size crossover scaling**, especially the distinction between a transition’s shifting location and its narrowing width. Note 28 already has both: a center approaching \(64\) and a much thinner transition layer.

Landau theory and correlation measurements could help determine whether there is additional critical behavior underneath that crossover. I would treat conformal symmetry and anomalous dimensions as hypotheses to test: the current notes establish neither a scale-invariant correlation theory nor a renormalization-group fixed point.

I’ve saved the review and literature note, including your order-parameter and correlation suggestions. The proposed next analytical task is now specific: define a connected correlation and response, then determine whether their scaling contains anything beyond the known carrier behavior and regulator crossover. The finite-source certification remains a separate task.

Yes—**an order parameter, connected correlations, and response functions** give us a more precise way to investigate your idea.

One distinction matters: at a continuous critical point, the **correlation length and susceptibility** may diverge while the connected two-point function develops long-range power-law behavior. The correlator need not diverge at a fixed separation. The susceptibility–correlation relation also requires an appropriate statistical or response framework. [Tong’s correlation discussion](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/sft/sfthtml/S2.html).

The project’s \(Q\) is a signed difference of local filtered gradient variances. It is not yet a separated-point correlation function or susceptibility. Establishing that connection would be worthwhile.

The **join** is the construction that combines the central finite-source approximation with the endpoint and outer-height formulas while preserving their equations. A time blend introduces an extra heat-equation residual; a spatial blend generally breaks holomorphy. A transition model could help construct a better approximation across the overlap, but these compatibility terms still require bounds.

There is already a concrete phase-transition analogy in Notes 27–28. At large height \(X\), the normalized density has different limiting profiles on either side of \(t=64\), although it remains smooth at every finite height. The transition has:

- A center displaced from \(64\) by approximately \(64/\log X\).
- A much narrower width of order \(1/(X\log X)\).

That distinction between **location shift and rounding width** closely matches the questions studied in [Fisher–Barber finite-size scaling](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.28.1516). However, this particular transition arises from the chosen regulator. It does not yet establish intrinsic critical behavior of the theta field.

The literature suggests this order of investigation:

| Tool | What it could contribute here |
|---|---|
| **Landau order parameter** | Identify a quantity distinguishing regimes, then derive its effective description and symmetries from the field. [Landau framework](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/sft/sfthtml/S1.html) |
| **Correlation and crossover scaling** | Separate growing correlations from ordinary amplitude growth and regulator-induced narrowing. |
| **RG, anomalous dimensions, CFT** | Constrain correlation scaling once a suitable scale transformation, fixed point, and symmetry structure are established. These premises remain open here. [Scaling and conformal symmetry](https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/sft/sfthtml/S3.html) |
| **Uniform asymptotics** | Construct a transition formula valid across regimes. Coalescing-saddle methods are candidates only if the actual saddle geometry satisfies their hypotheses. [DLMF methods](https://dlmf.nist.gov/2.4#v) |

On the original review, **Notes 35–37 make substantial quantitative progress**. Note 35 identifies the dominant errors; Note 36 improves their bounds; Note 37’s Hermite source and directional caps bring all sampled source allowances within budget at the two tested points. The worst ratio falls to **0.689 of its source allocation**. I found no blocking issue in the local analytic steps inspected.

The remaining obstacles are continuous arithmetic/integration certification, coverage beyond those two \(t=64\) observations, effective endpoint overlaps, and compatible global joining. The project has a promising finite approximation and endpoint theory, but no accepted global construction.
